intro: What each Challenge runs now, which version comes next, and what changes in it. Every change ships as a new version with its own board and its own crown. Nothing already graded is rescored. Mainnet started clean: no testnet registration, score or crown carries over.
next_label: Planned; final rules and values are published with each version, on its How you're tested page.

changes: Motor 1.8 is live on mainnet. Motor 1.9 is the next version; its opening is announced when it is set.

More of the motor is graded: every output that Carbon can solve for reference and that passes its pre-registered checks. Planned: torque and torque ripple, the open-circuit and loaded back-EMF, the mean torque in the cogging conditions, and the lowest flux density in the magnets (the demagnetization margin).
The zero point moves up: a class scores zero at the accuracy of Carbon's own quick, coarse reference solve, and one at reference accuracy. Credit goes only to models that beat a cheap solver.
Carbon publishes the coarse-solve results for every training design next to the reference results, so a model can learn the correction from coarse to fine.
Graph route only, and builds can use the GPU.

Why it's valuable: motor designers check torque, back-EMF and the risk of demagnetizing the magnets with slow magnetic-field solves, one design at a time. A fast model of all of them lets them search far more designs before building anything.

How it reaches for the state of the art: fast motor models are usually trusted only inside the range they were trained on, and only for torque. This version grades the full set of outputs a designer checks, beyond the training range, against a cheap solver rather than a curve fit.
The version planned for the Cooling mainnet launch; its opening is announced when it is set.
The first Cooling version with exam cases outside the training range. How far they reach is not published.

More of the cold plate is graded: the peak temperature and where it sits, the temperature profile along the channel, the outlet temperature and the pressure drop. The mean temperature is scored from your predicted profile.
The zero point is Carbon's own quick, coarse reference solve: a class scores zero at its accuracy and one at reference accuracy. Coarse-solve results are published for every training design.

Graph route only, and builds can use the GPU. The official build trains your recipe on the published training set only; the data kit is for practice and for checking your own solves against Carbon's reference cases.

Why it's valuable: cold plates for high-power chips are sized with slow conjugate heat-transfer solves, and the hottest spot on the die sets the limit. A fast model of the peak, the profile and the pressure drop lets engineers try many channel and fin layouts in minutes.

How it reaches for the state of the art: quick cooling estimates handle average temperatures well but miss narrow hot spots. This version grades where the peak sits and how hot it gets, including outside the training range, against a cheap solver rather than a curve fit.
One larger physics upgrade, joining mainnet once it passes its checks. The testnet Ribbed Bracket is rehearsal only.
The bracket is shaken through its mounting while carrying a payload, so its response depends on resonance, not only on stiffness.

Graded outputs are planned to include the natural frequencies of the lower modes, the tip deflection, and the static and dynamic stress at the fillet, averaged over a small patch so the reference is stable, with the frequency where that stress peaks. Each output is graded only if it passes its pre-registered checks.
The zero point is Carbon's own quick, coarse reference solve, and coarse-solve results are published for the training designs.
The material is a choice among alloys with published properties.

Why it's valuable: brackets that carry equipment on vibrating structures in vehicles, aircraft and machinery fail from resonance and from stress concentrated at fillets. Each check normally needs a modal and a dynamic analysis.

How it reaches for the state of the art: fast structural models mostly predict stiffness and static stress. Predicting the response near resonance, where a small change in the design swings the stress, is the harder problem this version is built around.
Burst Thermal launches on mainnet with 3.2 once it passes its checks; its opening is announced when it is set. Burst Thermal 3.0 and 3.1 will not open.

New in 3.2: the die is cooled by boiling. The heat transfer at the cooled face jumps when the liquid starts to boil and changes steeply with the local wall temperature, so part of the face can be boiling while the rest is not.
Bursts can come as two pulses, in the training set and in the exam, so the heat left from the first pulse matters for the second.
Carried over: materials whose properties change with temperature, and leakage power that rises with temperature, so a hot design can heat itself further.
The pulse shape is an input, and every design is checked against the peak temperature limit.
The zero point is Carbon's own quick, coarse reference solve, and coarse-solve results are published for the training designs.

Why it's valuable: chips run in bursts, and the peak temperature during a burst decides throttling and lifetime. Two-phase cold plates are used for the hottest chips because boiling removes heat far better, but only while it lasts.

How it reaches for the state of the art: simple thermal models assume one fixed cooling coefficient. This version asks for models that learn where and when the face boils, together with self-heating, which a single lumped coefficient cannot capture.

every_version: Score: half physics, half design value; on Motor 1.8, accuracy only from the switch time Carbon posts. Gates come first: a failed gate means no score.

Physics: your model is scored on hidden cases, many of them outside the training data, grouped into classes. On the new versions a class scores zero at the accuracy of Carbon's own quick, coarse reference solve and one at reference accuracy, so credit goes only to a model that beats a cheap solver. Each family of classes counts equally.
Every output that Carbon can solve for reference and that passes its pre-registered checks is graded.
Accuracy inside the training range is a gate: pass or fail, never points. Your model must clear it to be scored at all, but a smaller error there earns nothing extra.

Design value (only where the score line counts it): for each design task Carbon solves many candidate designs in advance and keeps them sealed. Your model predicts each one on its own; a sample of them then counts. Your top five picks in it are checked against the solved answers. Zero means no better than Carbon's classical picks on that sample.
If your model's predictions change with the batch it is shown, design value is zero for that grade; on Motor 1.8, from the switch time Carbon posts, that grade is not ranked.

The crown is decided on the official grade: a submission takes it when its official score beats the king's by the published margin and it passes every gate. Submissions are decided in queue order, and a tie keeps the king. There is no repeated rebuild before a crown changes hands.
On mainnet, Carbon builds your model on its own data-center GPU and grades it on its own machines. Timings close to a limit can differ from your own machine, so leave some headroom.
You see your total and status. Results per case or per part are not shown.
Data kits replace the shared practice banks: you generate your own practice data with Carbon's solver, and the training set is published as soon as it is frozen and checked, before the version opens.
fixes: Uploads to Motor on mainnet could time out while the validator was busy grading. A fix is live and uploads complete again. If an upload of yours failed, submit it again.
A graded model that ran out of a limit on the validator showed as not graded yet. It now shows as a candidate failure, naming the step that failed and the limit it hit. Update your install to see it.
known_issues: Motor is graded on mainnet (subnet 116) at version 1.8, and the test network's Motor door is closed. Cooling, Burst Thermal and Ribbed Bracket on the test network are rehearsal only; each joins mainnet at its new version. Miner files are not carried across a version or a network change: please re-upload (the app uploads your graph files from your project when you submit).

An older install shows a submission waiting for the validator as Refused: evaluation queued. Nothing was refused: it is queued, so don't submit again. Update your install and it reads Submitted, waiting for the validator's verdict.

Where a door publishes it, the dashboard shows that Challenge's queue: how many submissions are waiting and the typical wait. An updated install also shows your own place in line, the validator's state (up, paused, updating) and the typical wait in the Launchpad (Your place in line).

A build that runs out of time while the validator machine is busy can still count against the model. That is our fault, not yours, and it is being changed so such a run is retried. Until then, leave some headroom on time.
A catalog practice runs on the CPU, even on a GPU machine: catalog entries have no GPU build yet. Start from your own graph to practise on the GPU.
Close to a physics check, a practice that ran on the CPU can differ from the official grade, which always builds your model on the validator's GPU.
A 16 GB machine cannot run practice: Docker must see at least 17 GiB of memory.

faq.q: Does anything from testnet carry over to mainnet?
a: No. Mainnet starts clean: registrations, scores, crowns and submissions all start fresh. Testnet results are rehearsal only.
Your wallet works on both networks, but you register again on mainnet.

faq.q: Can I use constants learned from the training set?
a: Yes. What your model learns from the training set inside Carbon's build is not charged against the size budget on the graph route; the budget covers the graph itself and the constants you write into it.
There are no trained starting weights: everything trainable trains from scratch in Carbon's build, on the published training set only.
A branch that looks up stored answers for training rows is not allowed: it would make Carbon's own checks report a table instead of your model, and it gains no exam score.

faq.q: Why does my result show no total?
a: A result that does not count shows no total and says why. Not admitted: an invalid result, an ineligible design decision, or a score part below its required minimum. Not graded: an infrastructure problem or indeterminate evidence, which doesn't use your allowance.
On a board, a hotkey whose latest result does not count is in the Not scored count.

faq.q: Can I compare my practice total with my official grade?
a: No. Practice runs on your own data and kit cases; the official grade runs on hidden cases you never see, many of them outside the training range. A practice total is never an exam score or grade.

faq.q: How do I read the ladder?
a: Rank is the board's order: the leader first, then by exact score.
An = before a rank means those hotkeys share that rank.
Totals are shown rounded down to the Ladder step, so totals within one step show the same number.
Failed a gate lists hotkeys whose latest result failed a mandatory gate. A hotkey with an earlier scored result keeps its rank on that best result; the failed result is not scored.

faq.q: What is the score to beat?
a: Beat the king's official score by the margin, passing every gate and minimum, to take the crown.
With no king yet, you need to beat Carbon's baseline by the margin.
